newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Third World leaders slam unfair world trade rules.
newsitem.headline: Third World leaders slam unfair world trade rules.

text.p: Third World leaders opened a three-day trade promotion summit on Sunday, accusing industrialised states of frog-marching them into internationally binding trade pacts which erode their sovereignty.
In speeches at the Group of 15 meeting, Zimbabwean, Egyptian and Malaysian leaders called on the international community to implement agreed measures aimed at achieving fair world trade.

"Of concern to us is the urgency with which new issues are being forced onto the international trading agenda. This deliberate and expansive interpretation of the WTO (World Trade Organisation)'s remit needs to be checked," Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe said when he opened the (G-15) summit.

"The strong-arm tactics and the unrelenting pressure brought to bear on us confirm our suspicions that we are being frog- marched into internationally-binding arrangements that will eventually entail the total surrender of national sovereignty," he said.

In a scathing attack apparently directed at the United States, Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said one country was blatantly undermining the WTO by enacting extra-territorial laws to be submitted to by all nations and enterprises.

"We just cannot accept, and certainly cannot submit to such unilateral measures of coercion. We should take a firm position in containing these measures which arrogantly disregard the accepted norms and principles of international trade and investment relations" he said.

Malaysia's state oil company Petronas, faces U.S. sanctions for investing in Iran. It has a 30 percent stake in Iran's $600 million Sirri oilfields exploration project which puts it over the $40 million a year level the U.S. has said non-U.S. companies can invest in Iran and Libya's oil and gas sectors.
Malaysia has vowed to challenge the U.S. threat.

On Sunday, Mahathir said: "Developing countries must reject this challenge to their sovereign right to be free to trade and invest wherever they wish and which also threatens the expansion of trade and development, globally".
He said social clauses being promoted by the West to govern international trade were aimed at negating the advantage of cheap labour costs developing countries had over them.
Mahathir said globalisation of trade was being used to disadvantage developing countries which he said were expected to adopt policies and criteria unilaterally determined by the West.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said developing countries should consolidate their position ahead of the WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore from November 8 to 13 to ensure consideration of their trade concerns.

"Any arrangements or systems that would increase the gap between developed and developing countries we will refuse and refuse strongly. The outcome of the meeting must be to the advantage of the whole of developing countries," he said.

Although the G-15 still retains that name, it now comprises 16 countries, namely -- Algeria, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Jamaica, Malaysia, Mexico, Nigeria, Senegal, Peru, Venezuela, Yugoslavia and Zimbabwe.
